title: Blog 1
content:
Cleaning up AWS resources: The costs that continue after you “turn things off” AWS Study Group post: View the original post on Facebook Posted on: November 13, 2026.
The original post is written in Vietnamese for the AWS Study Group community. This page is the English version for my internship report.
After practicing on AWS, many people stop their EC2 instances or finish a lab and assume the costs stop too. In reality, AWS charges for each resource that still exists in the account, not only for whether a machine is running. This post summarizes the costs that are easy to miss, how AWS charges for each of them, and the clean-up order to follow.
Why “stopped” is not the same as “no charge” When an EC2 instance is stopped, AWS does not charge for instance usage. However, attached EBS volumes are still charged for storage, and Elastic IP addresses still incur charges regardless of the instance state.
In other words, the instance is only the compute part. Disks, IP addresses, and snapshots are separate resources with their own costs.
AWS Budgets: an alert, not a limit AWS Budgets tracks costs and sends notifications by email or Amazon SNS when a threshold is crossed. Two points are worth noting:
Budgets information is updated up to three times a day, so there is a delay between incurring a charge and receiving the alert. Budgets does not delete resources. To block spending automatically, you can configure a budget action that applies an IAM policy denying the creation of new resources once the threshold is reached. Costs that are easy to miss 1. NAT Gateway A NAT gateway is usually placed in a public subnet so that EC2 instances in a private subnet can reach the internet.
Source: AWS Documentation – NAT gateway use cases .
It is charged for every hour the NAT gateway is provisioned and available; a partial hour is billed as a full hour. There is also a data processing charge for each GB that passes through it. The pricing page example for US East (Ohio) is 0.045 USD per hour, or about 32.4 USD for 30 days, even with no traffic. If EC2 instances only need Amazon S3, a gateway VPC endpoint is the cheaper option because it has no hourly charge and no data processing charge.
2. Public IPv4 and Elastic IP Each public IPv4 address costs 0.005 USD per hour, the same whether it is attached to a resource or idle in the account; that is about 3.6 USD for 30 days. After deleting a NAT gateway or an EC2 instance, release the Elastic IP if it is no longer needed. Public IP Insights in Amazon VPC IP Address Manager shows the public IPv4 addresses the account holds. 3. EBS volumes, snapshots, and AMIs Deregistering an AMI does not delete its snapshots unless you choose to delete them at the same time. The remaining snapshots continue to incur storage charges. Clean-up order: terminate the instance, delete EBS volumes in the available state, deregister the AMI, then delete the snapshots. 4. AWS DMS replication instances A replication instance is charged by the hour, even after the migration task has finished. T3 replication instances run in unlimited mode: if average CPU utilization over 24 hours exceeds the baseline, extra CPU credit charges apply. 5. AWS Quick Sight Quick Sight (formerly Amazon QuickSight) is charged per user: an Author costs 24 USD per user per month. When it is no longer needed, cancel the subscription. This permanently deletes every dashboard, analysis, and dataset in all Regions, so do it only when the data does not need to be kept. 6. Amazon Athena and query results in S3 SQL queries are charged by the amount of data scanned. In the AWS example, a 3 TB uncompressed text table costs 15 USD per query (5 USD per TB); GZIP compression at 3:1 brings it down to 5 USD; converting to Parquet lets Athena read only the columns it needs, which lowers the cost further. Query results are stored in Amazon S3 and billed at S3 rates, so clean up the results bucket after practicing. Clean-up process after practicing Delete resources in dependency order: stop tasks or jobs first, then delete the underlying resources. Networking: delete the NAT gateway, release the Elastic IP, and delete VPC endpoints and VPN resources if any. Compute and storage: terminate EC2 instances, delete leftover EBS volumes, deregister AMIs, and delete snapshots. Data and analytics: delete databases and replication instances, cancel Quick Sight if unused, and clean up the S3 buckets that hold data and Athena results. Use AWS Resource Explorer with cross-Region search to find leftover resources in other Regions; searching is free of charge. Check Billing again the next day, because cost data is delayed. Applying consistent tags when creating resources, for example Project=lab-vpc, makes filtering and cleaning up faster.
A note on pricing Prices in this post come from the official AWS pricing pages at the time of writing (November 2026); some examples use the US East (Ohio) Region as shown on the pricing pages. Prices vary by Region and over time, so check them with AWS Pricing Calculator for the Region you use.

title: Blog 2
content:
IAM roles on EC2 and IMDSv2: Where does your application get its credentials? AWS Study Group post: View the original post on Facebook Posted on: November 17, 2026.
The original post is written in Vietnamese for the AWS Study Group community. This page is the English version for my internship report.
Applications running on EC2 often need to call AWS services such as Amazon S3 or DynamoDB. The quickest approach is to put an access key in the code or a configuration file, but an access key is a long-term credential. AWS recommends that workloads running on AWS use the temporary credentials of an IAM role, so there is no need to distribute long-lived access keys.
This post explains how EC2 receives IAM role credentials, how IMDSv2 works, and the configuration mistakes that are easy to make.
Instance profiles: the link between EC2 and an IAM role EC2 does not attach an IAM role directly. It uses an instance profile as a container for the role.
Source: AWS IAM User Guide – Use an IAM role to grant permissions to applications running on Amazon EC2 instances .
When you create a role in the IAM console, an instance profile with the same name is created automatically. With the AWS CLI or an SDK, you create the role and the instance profile separately. An instance profile contains only one IAM role; a role can be included in multiple instance profiles. To change an instance’s permissions, replace its instance profile. Removing a role from an instance profile can take up to one hour to take effect. The flow has four steps:
An admin creates an IAM role with the required permissions (for example, read access to an S3 bucket). A developer launches an EC2 instance with that role. The application retrieves the role credentials from inside the instance. The application uses those credentials to call S3. Where do the credentials come from? Credentials are provided by the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) at the link-local address 169.254.169.254, called from inside the instance:
/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name> The response contains AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, Token, and Expiration. Key points:
The credentials are temporary and rotated automatically by AWS; new credentials are available at least five minutes before the old ones expire. The AWS SDKs and AWS CLI retrieve these credentials automatically, so the application code does not need to contain an access key. IMDS queries are throttled per instance. Cache the credentials until they approach expiry instead of calling IMDS on every request. How does IMDSv2 work? By default, an instance accepts both IMDSv1 (a simple request/response method) and IMDSv2 (session-oriented, requires a token). IMDSv2 has two steps:
Step 1 – Get a token with PUT, specifying the token lifetime (from one second to six hours):
TOKEN=$(curl -sf -X PUT "http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token" \ -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600") Step 2 – Send GET requests with the token in a header:
curl -sf -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \ http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ Token rules:
A token is bound to the instance that created it and does not work anywhere else. A token can be reused until it expires; after that, send another PUT to get a new one. A GET with an invalid or expired token returns 401 Unauthorized. Why is IMDSv2 more secure? According to the AWS Security Blog, IMDSv2 adds protection for scenarios where requests are relayed to IMDS from outside:
Open WAFs: most WAFs do not pass PUT requests, so they cannot open an IMDSv2 session. Open reverse proxies: proxies usually add the X-Forwarded-For header; IMDSv2 rejects PUT requests that contain it. SSRF: the attacker must both send a PUT and include the secret token in the headers of later GET requests; most SSRF vulnerabilities cannot do both. Open firewalls, NATs, routers, and VPNs: the token response has an IP hop limit (TTL) of 1, so it is discarded before it leaves the instance. A limit to keep in mind: requests made from the instance itself can still get a token. IMDSv2 does not replace least privilege for the IAM role, because code running on the instance can still use the role’s permissions.
Common configuration mistakes 1. Containers cannot get a token The default hop limit for the PUT response is 1. A container running on EC2 adds a network hop, so it may not receive the token. Some AWS SDKs retry and then fall back to IMDSv1, which causes delays. AWS recommends raising the hop limit to 2 in container environments.
2. A curl script “succeeds” but the token is an error message When IMDS returns an error, curl still returns a success status and stores the error message in the TOKEN variable. Use the -f option so that curl returns an error status and the script stops at the right point.
3. Services that make HTTP calls on the application’s behalf HTTP proxies, HTML/CSS validator services, and XML processors that support XML inclusion can expose credentials if they make HTTP requests on behalf of the application.
4. An account-level default is set, but older instances still use IMDSv1 Setting IMDSv2 as the account-level default does not change existing instances; each instance must be updated.
Requiring IMDSv2 At launch: in the console, choose Metadata version = V2 only (token required); with the AWS CLI, set HttpTokens=required and HttpEndpoint=enabled:
aws ec2 run-instances ... \ --metadata-options "HttpEndpoint=enabled,HttpTokens=required,HttpPutResponseHopLimit=2" Account level (per Region): set V2 only as the default for new instances, and optionally turn on Enforce IMDSv2 to block launching instances that do not require IMDSv2.
Before switching: make sure applications no longer depend on IMDSv1 and that SDK/CLI versions support IMDSv2.
Key takeaways Use an IAM role and instance profile instead of access keys on EC2. Role credentials are temporary, rotated automatically, and retrieved through IMDS. IMDSv2 uses session tokens: PUT to get a token, GET with the token. Require IMDSv2, set the hop limit to 2 for containers, and keep the role’s permissions to a minimum. References AWS IAM User Guide — Security best practices in IAM AWS IAM User Guide — Use an IAM role to grant permissions to applications running on Amazon EC2 instances (diagram source) Amazon EC2 User Guide — IAM roles for Amazon EC2 Amazon EC2 User Guide — Retrieve security credentials from instance metadata Amazon EC2 User Guide — Use the Instance Metadata Service to access instance metadata Amazon EC2 User Guide — Access instance metadata for an EC2 instance Amazon EC2 User Guide — Configure instance metadata options for new instances AWS Security Blog — Add defense in depth against open firewalls, reverse proxies, and SSRF vulnerabilities with enhancements to the EC2 Instance Metadata Service #AWS #AmazonEC2 #AWSIAM #IMDSv2 #CloudSecurity #AWSStudyGroup #FirstCloudJourney

Order Speaker Position Presentation topics 1 Eric Yeo Country General Manager, Malaysia, Vietnam & Indochina, AWS Cloud and AI adoption in Vietnam, with examples from businesses. 2 Werner Vogels CTO, Amazon Engineering decisions behind cloud services, including databases, compute infrastructure, and time synchronization. 3 Jens Lottner CEO, Techcombank Bringing AI into banking operations and preparing employees to work with it. 4 Mai Le Director of Product Management, Katalon Software validation during development with AI and human responsibility for the results. 5 Trung Nguyen Technical Account Manager, AWS Vietnam Joint presentation of AWS Security Agent: Proactive AppSec from Design to Deployment. 6 Tan Huynh Technical Account Manager, AWS Vietnam Joint presentation of AWS Security Agent and the security testing workflow. 7 Hoàng Minh Deputy Minister of Science and Technology Opening remarks at the event. 8 Jennifer Wicks U.S. Ambassador to Vietnam Technology cooperation, digital infrastructure, and workforce development. Key highlights Opening and AI adoption in Vietnam Eric Yeo opened the program, introduced the guests and speakers, and thanked the event partners. Deputy Minister Hoàng Minh and Ambassador Jennifer Wicks then delivered their remarks. Jennifer Wicks discussed the role of cloud computing in business, technology cooperation between Vietnam and the United States, and the development of infrastructure and workforce skills.
Returning to the stage, Eric Yeo spoke about AWS’s twentieth anniversary and the AWS Local Zone in Hanoi. He introduced examples from several industries: OmiGroup’s research into chronic diseases with links to medical evidence, Vinasoy’s monitoring of retail product displays, and Agris’s use of data across agricultural operations. These examples helped me understand the specific problems each business wanted to address with Cloud and AI.
Techcombank: preparing the platform and people to use AI Jens Lottner explained how Techcombank organizes AI adoption. Building on its existing data foundation and AWS services, the bank added a platform for coordinating agents, workflows, access permissions, and controls. Employees can use prepared agents or build workflows suited to their own tasks.
One example that caught my attention was AI Coach, which helps employees select models, write requests, and consider usage costs. The presentation also covered training at different skill levels so employees can use and operate these tools.
Three areas of application were introduced: software development, incident coordination, and support for staff working with customers. In the incident example, an agent coordinates information between operations and customer-facing teams so remediation and customer updates can proceed together. At the end of his presentation, Jens Lottner discussed cost, return on investment, talent, and risk management. These are questions I also need to consider when choosing a problem to explore with AI.
The FCAJ community and a greeting to Ho Chi Minh City Eric Yeo continued with AWS training activities, First Cloud and AI Journey, and AWS Academy. He shared stories of people who started learning cloud, secured internships, and returned to support the community. This part related closely to my own internship, where learning needs practical work and opportunities to speak with more experienced people.
Before inviting Werner Vogels onto the stage, Eric Yeo greeted the community watching the livestream in Ho Chi Minh City. I wanted to record this moment because my team was attending at that location.
Werner Vogels: the engineering behind cloud services Werner Vogels recalled a database incident during a peak shopping period at Amazon. By reviewing how applications accessed their data, the team found that many needs could be served by a key-value model. His example of retrieving a shopping cart by customer ID helped me understand why actual query patterns matter when choosing a database.
He then presented three stories about improvements behind the services:
AWS Nitro: Moving much of the I/O work to dedicated hardware reduces the burden on the hypervisor and improves isolation. This example showed how an infrastructure change can affect both performance and security. Lambda, Firecracker, and SnapStart: Starting with the need to process a file uploaded to S3, the presentation explored running small functions with suitable isolation and cost. Firecracker was introduced through its microVM approach, while SnapStart was explained through saving initialized state to reduce startup time. Time synchronization: He described the difficulty of ordering events across multiple machines and how AWS provides accurate time with explicit error bounds. I want to study this further when learning about data and distributed systems. These examples made the work behind familiar actions, such as creating a virtual machine or running a Lambda function, easier to understand. When studying a service, I need to understand the problem it solves and the conditions that affect its use.
Katalon: validating software as AI generates code faster Mai Le began with a familiar coding-agent interaction: the user points out an error, and the agent agrees to correct it. She used this to introduce the gap between the speed of software creation and the capacity to validate it. When testing falls behind, errors can reach end users.
The presentation described connecting requirements, code changes, tests, execution results, defects, and production data to assess a release. Agents need this context to identify changes, select what to test, run the tests, and gather evidence. People remain responsible for setting risk boundaries, reviewing exceptions, and approving releases.
Mai Le also described the roles of Amazon EKS, RDS, S3, and Kinesis in Katalon’s platform, alongside Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore Runtime for its AI capabilities. The point I want to apply to my own work is to keep actual verification results, such as logs, screenshots, and test outcomes, so I can explain why a feature meets its requirements.
To close the keynote, Werner Vogels returned to the validation work that can accumulate as more code is generated, and to engineers’ professional responsibility. He spoke about work that users rarely see but that still requires care. I connected this with error handling, testing, and resource cleanup in my own workshop.
AI-DLC and how TCBS organizes work for agents I kept photos of the comparison between traditional SDLC and AI-DLC, along with the workspace diagram from TCBS. In the diagram, an orchestrator prepares and monitors workspaces for individual agents and tasks. Each workspace includes a task package, source code, MCP tools, verification steps, and a checkpoint.
What I want to learn from this example is how to prepare a task before assigning it to AI. If the requirement and completion criteria are unclear, it is also difficult for me to judge the result. I can start by defining the inputs, outputs, and checks for each small feature in my workshop.
AWS Security Agent and security testing during development Session DVT305, presented by Trung Nguyen and Tan Huynh, covered application security from design through deployment. One slide outlined a workflow involving login, scanning, execution of testing tasks, further exploration based on findings, and resource cleanup.
This made me pay closer attention to the scope of a test: which system is being tested, what permissions are needed, and which resources must be removed afterward. These are also details I need to explain clearly in an AWS workshop. The session gave me subjects to explore, while applying them will require reading the documentation and practicing each step.
Agent Toolkit for AWS and MCP The Agent Toolkit for AWS slides introduced ways to give coding agents tools, knowledge, and controls. The getting started sequence covered installing a plugin, checking the connection to the AWS MCP Server, and trying a specific request. I also photographed the slide containing QR codes for the source repository and further reading.
I am interested in where an agent gets its information and which actions it can perform. When I try these tools after the event, I want to begin with a small task, read the changes it produces, and check the outcome before expanding the scope.
Key takeaways Prepare the requirement before using AI Divide work into tasks with clear outputs. Provide source code, documentation, and constraints relevant to the task. Decide how to check the result before starting. Take responsibility for the result Read and understand changes proposed by AI before including them in my work. Test successful behavior and error cases. Keep practice results so I can explain my decisions. Choose an approach based on the actual problem Understand how data will be read and written before choosing a database. When trying AI, consider usage costs, access permissions, and the time needed to check results. Make time to learn the tools and assess their output, as illustrated by the employee training in Techcombank’s presentation. Include security in the practice plan Review permissions and resource scope before running a tool. Include verification and cleanup steps in the workshop instructions. Learn the limits of tools, especially those able to act on an AWS environment. Applying to work I plan to begin with my personal workshop. For each feature, I will write a short requirement, identify the expected outcome, and define a check before asking AI for help. I will then review the changes, run the exercise, and record the results in my worklog.
For MCP and Agent Toolkit for AWS, I want to try a task in a practice environment with a defined scope. I will record the setup, any problems encountered, and the checks I complete after trying it.
Following the keynote, I also want to add a short explanation of data access patterns and service choices to my workshop design. For each feature change, I will retain the original requirement, the changes made, and verification evidence to refer to when preparing my report or demo.
Event experience Following the program with my team in Ho Chi Minh City The watch party let me follow the program with my teammates at the AWS office in Ho Chi Minh City. Our photo collection includes a group picture with attendance badges and photos of technical sessions on screen. Looking back through them helps me connect each point in this report to a specific presentation.
What I want to explore next The TCBS workspace diagram is an example I want to revisit when dividing up project work. The testing and security sessions also reminded me to make time for checks after writing code. My next step is to choose a small part to try, record the results, and then decide whether it belongs in my workshop.

title: Blog 3
content:
Amazon RDS: Multi-AZ or read replica? Choosing between high availability and read scaling AWS Study Group post: View the original post on Facebook Posted on: November 23, 2026.
The original post is written in Vietnamese for the AWS Study Group community. This page is the English version for my internship report.
Amazon RDS offers three deployment options that keep a replica of the data in another Availability Zone (AZ): Multi-AZ DB instance, Multi-AZ DB cluster, and read replica. They serve two different goals:
High availability (HA): when the primary instance fails, the application switches to the copy and keeps running. Read scaling: move read queries off the primary instance to reduce its load. The differences come down to three points: the replication mode, the failover mechanism, and whether the copy serves read traffic.
The three options at a glance Multi-AZ DB instance Multi-AZ DB cluster Read replica Main purpose High availability High availability + reads Read scaling Replication Synchronous Semisynchronous Asynchronous Copy serves reads No Yes (2 readers) Yes Failover Automatic, typically 60–120 seconds Automatic, typically under 35 seconds Manual (promote) Placement 2 AZs in one Region 3 AZs in one Region Same AZ, another AZ, or another Region Engines MariaDB, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server MySQL, PostgreSQL MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2 Multi-AZ DB instance: one standby, for failover only RDS automatically provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in another AZ. Each change on the primary is written to the standby before it is acknowledged.
The standby does not serve reads. According to the AWS documentation, this is not a read scaling solution; to read from a copy, use a Multi-AZ DB cluster or a read replica. Failover through DNS: RDS changes the DNS record of the endpoint to point to the standby. Failover typically takes 60–120 seconds, and can take longer with large transactions or a lengthy recovery. The application must reconnect after failover. When automatic failover happens: OS patching during the maintenance window, an unhealthy or unreachable primary host, a busy and unresponsive primary, a failed storage volume, or Reboot with failover. Backups are taken from the standby, which avoids the brief I/O suspension on the primary when a snapshot starts. Trade-off: synchronous replication increases write and commit latency compared with Single-AZ. AWS recommends Provisioned IOPS for production. MariaDB, MySQL, Oracle, and PostgreSQL use Amazon failover technology; SQL Server uses Database Mirroring or Always On Availability Groups. You can convert a running Single-AZ instance to Multi-AZ by modifying the instance and enabling the Multi-AZ option.
Multi-AZ DB cluster: two readable standbys A Multi-AZ DB cluster has one writer and two readers in three separate AZs in the same Region. It is not the same as an Aurora DB cluster.
Source: Amazon RDS User Guide – Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments for Amazon RDS .
Semisynchronous replication: a change is committed once at least one reader acknowledges it; it does not wait for every reader to apply it. Readers serve reads and are failover targets. When the writer fails, RDS promotes the reader with the most recent change record. Failover typically takes under 35 seconds. Three kinds of endpoint: Cluster (writer) endpoint: connects to the writer and is the only endpoint for write statements (DML, DDL). Reader endpoint (its name contains -ro): spreads connections across the readers and allows only read statements. Instance endpoints: point to each instance, mainly for diagnosis. Replica lag affects failover time: RDS must resolve the lag before it promotes a new writer. Lag usually grows with high write concurrency, heavy reads on the readers, or large transactions and DDL. Monitor it with the CloudWatch metric ReplicaLag. Limits to know: only MySQL and PostgreSQL, and only certain instance classes (for example db.m6gd, db.r6gd, db.c6gd); no stopping or starting the cluster, storage autoscaling, option groups, Kerberos, IPv6 dual-stack, or cross-Region automated backups. Read replica: an asynchronous copy for read scaling RDS creates a read replica from a snapshot of the source instance, then uses the engine’s built-in asynchronous replication to apply changes.
Source: Amazon RDS User Guide – Working with DB instance read replicas .
How many: up to 15 read replicas per MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server instance; up to 5 for Oracle. Autoscaling the number of replicas is not supported. Read-only: a replica accepts only read-only connections. MySQL and MariaDB replicas can be made writable, but writing to a replica is not recommended. Lag: because replication is asynchronous, data on the replica can be behind the source. Monitor ReplicaLag; for MySQL and MariaDB, a value of -1 means replication is not active. Cross-Region: a replica can live in another Region, to serve reads close to users or as a disaster recovery option. Manual promotion: promoting turns the replica into a standalone, writable DB instance. RDS stops replication and reboots the replica, which takes several minutes or longer depending on size. After promotion it cannot become a replica again. Requirement: the source instance must have automated backups enabled (a retention period other than 0). Cost: a replica is billed as a standard DB instance at its instance class rate. There is no charge for data transfer between the source and the replica within the same Region. A read replica can enable Multi-AZ itself to get its own standby, independent of whether the source is Multi-AZ.
Combining Multi-AZ and read replicas The two mechanisms are not mutually exclusive. A common architecture:
The source instance uses Multi-AZ to survive an AZ failure: a synchronous standby with automatic failover. Add read replicas for dashboards, reports, and heavy queries, so they do not affect the write path. Add a cross-Region read replica (with Multi-AZ on the replica if needed) for a Region-wide outage, accepting manual promotion. Application requirements Connect through endpoints, not IP addresses. The IP behind an endpoint changes on failover. Keep the DNS cache short. AWS recommends a JVM DNS TTL of no more than 60 seconds (networkaddress.cache.ttl=60). Connection pools should drop old connections after failover. Reconnect and retry, because existing connections are dropped during failover. Separate reads from writes: always write through the writer endpoint; queries that need the latest data should also read from the writer; only queries that tolerate lag (reports, statistics) should read from readers or replicas. Monitor ReplicaLag and set a CloudWatch alarm when it crosses a threshold. Test failover before you need it: Reboot with failover for a Multi-AZ DB instance, or aws rds failover-db-cluster for a Multi-AZ DB cluster. The Multi-AZ instance failover completed event is the authoritative sign that failover is done. Choosing by requirement The database just needs to survive an AZ failure: Multi-AZ DB instance. You need faster failover, lower write latency, and reads from the standbys, on MySQL or PostgreSQL: Multi-AZ DB cluster. Read queries overload the primary and can tolerate data a few seconds old: read replicas. You need a plan for a Region-wide outage: a cross-Region read replica, accepting manual promotion. Important production workloads: combine Multi-AZ for HA with read replicas for reads. Summary Multi-AZ is for surviving failures; read replicas are for sharing load. Multi-AZ DB instance: synchronous standby, not readable, automatic failover in 60–120 seconds. Multi-AZ DB cluster: 1 writer + 2 readers in 3 AZs, semisynchronous, failover typically under 35 seconds. Read replica: asynchronous, can lag, promoted manually, can be in another Region. The application must use endpoints, keep a short DNS TTL, reconnect, and monitor ReplicaLag. References Amazon RDS User Guide — Configuring and managing a Multi-AZ deployment for Amazon RDS Amazon RDS User Guide — Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS Amazon RDS User Guide — Failing over a Multi-AZ DB instance for Amazon RDS Amazon RDS User Guide — Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments for Amazon RDS (source of the Multi-AZ DB cluster diagram) Amazon RDS User Guide — Connecting to a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS Amazon RDS User Guide — Failing over a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS Amazon RDS User Guide — Limitations of Multi-AZ DB clusters for Amazon RDS Amazon RDS User Guide — Working with DB instance read replicas (source of the read replica and standby diagram) Amazon RDS User Guide — Promoting a read replica to be a standalone DB instance Amazon RDS User Guide — Monitoring read replication Amazon RDS Read Replicas #AWS #AmazonRDS #HighAvailability #MultiAZ #ReadReplica #CloudArchitecture #AWSStudyGroup #FirstCloudJourney

content:
This section lists the blogs I have posted to AWS Study Group .
Blog 1 - Cleaning up AWS resources: The costs that continue after you “turn things off” A summary based on the official AWS documentation and pricing pages: why “stopped” resources can still be billed, the costs that are easy to miss (NAT gateways, public IPv4, snapshots and AMIs, DMS, Quick Sight, Athena), the limits of AWS Budgets, and a clean-up process after practicing.
Blog 2 - IAM roles on EC2 and IMDSv2: Where does your application get its credentials? How an instance profile delivers temporary IAM role credentials to EC2 through the Instance Metadata Service, the IMDSv2 token flow (PUT for a token, GET with the token), why IMDSv2 reduces the risk from SSRF and open proxies, common configuration mistakes, and how to require IMDSv2.
Blog 3 - Amazon RDS: Multi-AZ or read replica? Choosing between high availability and read scaling A comparison of Multi-AZ DB instances (synchronous standby, not readable), Multi-AZ DB clusters (one writer and two readers in three AZs, semisynchronous replication), and read replicas (asynchronous, manually promoted, can be cross-Region): how they replicate and fail over, their limits, how to combine them, and what the application must do to handle failover.

Summary Report: “Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels” Event information Event Name: Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels
Date & Time: 08:30 a.m. to 12:00 p.m., Friday, October 2, 2026 (UTC+7)
Location: AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City
Attendance Format: In person
Role: Attendee
Just a few days earlier, I had watched Dr. Werner Vogels’ keynote on a screen at the AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi watch party. On October 2, I had the opportunity to hear him in person at the AWS office in Ho Chi Minh City. As someone studying Cloud and starting an internship, meeting Amazon’s CTO was an honor and a memorable experience.
Attendance objectives Hear Dr. Werner Vogels’ experience of building and operating systems at scale. Explore perspectives on Cloud, AI, and the skills needed in engineering. Connect what I learned with preparing my workshop and studying during the internship. Attend a community conversation in person with other AWS learners and practitioners in Ho Chi Minh City. Speakers Order Speaker Position 1 Dr. Werner Vogels VP and Chief Technology Officer, Amazon 2 Hung Gia Nguyen Head of Solutions Architect, AWS Vietnam and Cambodia 3 My Nguyen Solutions Architect, AWS Vietnam Topics and reflections after the event Hearing directly from an experienced practitioner The Fireside Chat centered on Cloud, AI, technology innovation, and experience building systems at scale. I attended as a learner, hoping to understand how someone with extensive experience approaches problems I am only beginning to explore.
What I wanted to take away was a clearer direction for my studies. Alongside learning how to use AWS services, I need to explain why I choose a service, which need it serves, and what could happen when something fails. These questions give me a starting point for further reading and practice.
Seeing a feature as part of a system I want to understand how the parts of an application depend on one another. A change to data storage or request processing can affect other parts of the system, so I need to consider those connections when making a design decision.
For my personal workshop, I want to trace a request from start to finish. Where does the data arrive, how is it processed, where is it stored, and how is the result returned? If one step fails, how does it affect the others? Drawing this flow will help me understand my work and explain it more clearly.
Taking responsibility when using AI I am responsible for the code I use, including code suggested by AI. I can ask a tool for an approach or an explanation of an error, but I need to review and check its output before including it in my own work.
I want to develop the habit of explaining the code I use. When I do not understand a piece of logic, I will study it further, run it, and check error cases. This should also help me recognize gaps in my knowledge.
Developing depth and communicating with others At this stage of my internship, I need to spend time on AWS fundamentals while learning how applications, data, and security fit together. I also need to practice explaining my work so that others can understand my choices and give useful feedback.
When working with my team or speaking with a mentor, I want to describe a problem in a way that is easy to follow: the goal, what I tried, the result, and where I am stuck. Preparing that information should make the discussion more specific and useful.
Key takeaways Understand before choosing: Start with the need and workflow, then choose the technology. Check error cases: Once a feature works, examine how it responds to missing data or a failed processing step. Take responsibility for my work: Review, test, and explain the parts developed with AI assistance. Keep learning regularly: Choose something I do not yet understand, practice it, and record the result. Communicate clearly: Describe the goal, completed work, and help needed when working with others. Applying to work While preparing my workshop, I plan to draw the data flow and briefly explain why I chose each AWS service. For every feature, I will prepare a successful case and an error case to test.
When using AI assistance, I will keep the original requirement, review the changes, and run them before adding them to the instructions. I will record technical decisions, errors, and solutions in my worklog so I can revisit them.
I also want to practice explaining my work to teammates. If I struggle to explain a component or a choice, that will identify an area to study before completing the demo.
Event experience A memorable opportunity during my internship Meeting Dr. Werner Vogels in person made this event particularly meaningful to me. As an attendee, I had the opportunity to hear from someone with many years of experience in Cloud and large distributed systems. It gave me more motivation to continue studying this field.
I appreciate the time he took to visit the AWS office and share his experience with the community. For me, a practical way to respond to that opportunity is to take my studies and project work seriously, starting with small tasks that I can understand, test, and explain myself.

title: Event 4
content:
Summary Report: “FCAJ Community Day” Event information Event Name: FCAJ Community Day
Date & Time: 09:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m., Saturday, October 31, 2026 (UTC+7)
Location: AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Ho Chi Minh City
Attendance Format: In person
Role: Attendee
Event Page: FCAJ Community Day on Luma FCAJ Community Day was a sharing session for the First Cloud AI Journey community, with six short talks over one morning. The topics ranged from AI-assisted software development and an AWS learning path for students to serverless architecture, asynchronous processing, a three-month internship story, and open source contribution. At the time I was in week 7 of my internship, so many of the sessions were closely related to what I was studying.
Attendance objectives Hear practical experience from people who have built and operated systems on AWS. Learn more about serverless services and asynchronous system design before starting my personal workshop. Learn from interns who had already completed the program. Meet and talk with other members of the FCAJ community. Agenda and speakers Time Session Speaker 09:00 – 09:25 Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories Henry (Duc) Bui, Head of Engineering at CloudThinker 09:30 – 09:55 New to AWS? Where should you start? Tuan Tran (Tran Minh Tuan), Backend Developer, FPT University – FCAJ 10:00 – 10:25 AWS Lambda Web Functions: Rethinking Serverless Web Architecture Thinh Nguyen, DevSecOps/Cloud Engineer at STYL Solutions, First Cloud AI Journey 10:30 – 11:00 Amazon SQS: Building Asynchronous Systems Dao Luong, FCAJ 11:00 – 11:25 My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey Khang Duong, FCAJ 11:30 – 12:00 Start & Maintain Consistency with Open Source Contributing Hung Tran, NAB The agenda comes from the event page on Luma. Speaker names and organizations come from the organizers’ speaker graphic and the title slide of each session.
Key highlights 1. Lessons from building “software factories” The opening session shared how the CloudThinker team organizes development with many AI agent sessions running in parallel. The title slide showed the number of merges into the develop branch each month, rising from 39 in December 2024 to about 2,900 in the last month on the chart. A volume of changes like this is only manageable when checks are fast and reliable.
Two ideas I noted:
One shared control folder: every session starts in a control folder that holds notes, skills, and machine guides. From there, the agent reaches the app, infrastructure, and docs repositories, team machines, and the dev and prod clusters as needed. A shared test cache: test results are stored by test and by a hash of the files the test uses. If the code is unchanged, the result is reused; if it changed, the test runs once and the result is saved for every session, while 2% of tests are re-run at random to verify the cache. A shared check runner also keeps 10 copies of the app ready and picks, from 65 checks (type checks, lint, migrations, secret scan, dependency audit, and tests), only those related to what changed. According to the slide, this reuses up to 72% of tests in a day and cuts the wait for checks by 76%. Figure 1. The session Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories by Henry (Duc) Bui.
Figure 2. Every agent session starts in one shared control folder.
Figure 3. A test cache and check runner shared by many sessions.
2. New to AWS? Where should you start? The session New to AWS? Where should you start? (listed as Education in the agenda) was aimed at students who are new to AWS and covered three things: three learning websites, a clear learning path, and AWS credit opportunities. The speaker stressed that no single website covers every learning need, so the three should be used together:
Website Purpose Main content AWS Study Group Hands-on practice Step-by-step workshops with instructions in Vietnamese AWS Skill Builder Structured learning Digital courses, exam preparation, labs, and topic-based resources AWS Builder Center Community and rewards Articles, workshops, student verification, and badges During the session, AWS Builder Center was opened live on screen to show its Spotlight section, events, and community activities. I realized that I had used many AWS Study Group lab sites but had not yet made use of Skill Builder or Builder Center.
Figure 4. Tuan Tran’s session for students who are starting with AWS.
Figure 5. Three learning websites that complement each other.
Figure 6. A live walkthrough of AWS Builder Center.
3. AWS Lambda Web Functions This session presented a new way to think about serverless web architecture with AWS Lambda Web Functions. According to the agenda and the AWS announcement, the main points were native HTTP support that lets a function run a standard HTTP server, up to 128 concurrent requests per execution environment, removing the adapter layer, Active CPU Billing, which meters only the CPU time the code actually uses so that waiting on a database or an external API costs little, and live benchmarks comparing it with running Docker on EC2/ECS.
In Lab22, I used Lambda to stop and start EC2 instances automatically with the traditional model, where each execution environment handles one event at a time. This session showed me that Lambda can also act as a real web server, and that the billing model is another factor to compare when choosing between serverless and containers.
Figure 7. The AWS Lambda Web Functions session by Thinh Nguyen.
4. Building asynchronous systems with Amazon SQS Dao Luong’s SQS session started from a simple example: a user asks for content to be generated, and an API service calls an AI service that uses Amazon Bedrock and then waits for the response. With synchronous processing, each step must finish before the next can continue. If the AI service is slow or unavailable, the request hangs or times out, and the user is forced to wait.
The solution is to put requests into an Amazon SQS queue to decouple the components: the API accepts the request and responds right away, while the heavy work runs in the background and scales independently. The session also covered design patterns and practical tips for implementation. I had not used SQS in my labs before, and I want to consider it for long-running tasks in my workshop.
Figure 8. Dao Luong explaining the problem with synchronous processing when a downstream service is slow or unavailable.
5. A three-month AWS internship journey Khang Duong shared the architecture of a real project after three months of internship: a multiplayer game built with Amplify, an HTTP API and a WebSocket API, Lambda functions that handle matches, SQS (including a delayed queue to handle timeouts), a schedule that rebuilds the ranking, DynamoDB for data, and Cognito for user authentication. The architecture spans two AWS accounts connected through AssumeRole, with an IAM role, Secrets Manager, a KMS key, CloudWatch, and X-Ray.
What stood out to me was that this architecture reuses many services I studied in Modules 05 to 07 (IAM, KMS, Lambda, DynamoDB), but combines them to solve a specific problem with proper monitoring and security. This is the level of completeness I want to aim for in my own workshop.
Figure 9. Khang Duong presenting the project architecture after three months of internship.
6. Starting and keeping up open source contributions The final session, by Hung Tran from NAB, explained how to find a starting point for open source contributions. The easiest way is to pick clear and simple issues, which are usually labeled good first issue, triaged, or ready to implement. The speaker’s favorite type of contribution is a batch change or refactor: a large change that already has a clear template, so newcomers can take on small parts of it. The two examples were migrating the Kubelet codebase to contextual logging (kubernetes#130069 ) and converting net.IP to netip.Addr in Cilium (cilium#24246 ).
The rest of the session covered building a steady contribution habit and how it benefits skills and career growth.
Figure 10. Hung Tran recommending clear and simple issues as a starting point.
Figure 11. Batch changes with a clear template are a good entry point for newcomers.
Key takeaways Automate checks before speeding up changes: Moving faster only helps when each change can still be verified, and the checks themselves need to be optimized so they do not slow the team down. Do not make every call synchronous: For slow or failure-prone tasks, a queue such as SQS keeps the system responsive and more fault tolerant. Compare costs when choosing an architecture: Serverless and containers differ in both performance and billing, so the choice needs actual measurements and estimates. Combine learning sources: Use AWS Study Group for practice, Skill Builder for structured learning, and Builder Center to connect with the community. Start small and stay consistent: This applies both to open source contributions and to self-study during the internship. Applying to work When designing my personal workshop, I will identify the processing steps that may be slow or fail and consider decoupling them with Amazon SQS instead of calling them directly. When choosing between Lambda and containers, I will record the reasons and estimate the cost of each option in the COST section.
I plan to create accounts on AWS Skill Builder and AWS Builder Center to fill gaps in my knowledge and follow community articles. I also want to look for a good first issue in a cloud-related open source project to get familiar with the contribution process.
Event experience The morning moved quickly with six sessions in a row, but each one offered a different perspective: engineering leaders and engineers working in industry, and members of the FCAJ community sharing their learning and projects. The session on the three-month internship journey gave me extra motivation, since that is exactly the path I am on now.
I attended with my FCAJ teammates and we had time to talk and take photos together after the sessions.
Figure 12. My check-in photo with members of the FCAJ community at the event on October 31, 2026. All images in this report come from my personal event photo collection.

title: Event 5
content:
Summary Report: “AWSxFPTU Cloud Mastery 1” Event information Event Name: AWSxFPTU Cloud Mastery 1
Date: Saturday, November 14, 2026
Location: AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City
Attendance Format: In person
Role: Attendee
AWSxFPTU Cloud Mastery 1 was a workshop for FPT University students built around one question: how do you take an AI application from a prototype to an enterprise production environment that is secure, reliable, and scalable? The content moved from general principles to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and ended with a demo of a real architecture. The event took place at the end of week 9, right after I had started narrowing down my workshop topic and sketching its architecture, so it was a good chance to check my direction.
Attendance objectives Understand the gap between an AI prototype and an AI system that runs reliably in an enterprise. Learn about Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the components that help bring AI agents to production. See how security, monitoring, and cost control fit into a real architecture. Take away points to consider for my personal workshop architecture. Agenda and speakers Part Topic Speaker 1 From Prototype to Production: Secure, Reliable, Scalable Enterprise AI on the Cloud Khang Duong, FCAJ member 2 AI in Enterprise: Enterprise Challenges and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Nguyen Lam Anh, AI Engineer, FCAJ 3 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore components: Identity, Gateway, Memory, and Observability To be updated 4 Demo: agent orchestration with Strands Agents, observability with Langfuse, and the deployment architecture on AWS To be updated The event has no public event page. Session titles and speakers come from the slides shown at the event.
Key highlights 1. From Prototype to Production Khang Duong’s opening part covered four sections: the gap between a prototype and production (The Gap), the four pillars of an enterprise AI system (The Four Pillars), how AWS addresses them (The AWS Answer), and what comes next (The Road Ahead).
The whole part was told through the story of a restaurant: a prototype is a home kitchen, enterprise AI is a restaurant chain, and the cloud is the central kitchen that serves the chain. In an enterprise, data is the ingredients, the AI model is the chef, the feature is the dish, and users are the customers. AI rarely stands alone; it is a feature inside the product, such as recommendations, a support chatbot, or fraud detection.
The two pillars I noted most clearly:
Security: AWS KMS keeps the “recipes” and customer information secret, IAM controls who enters the storeroom and who cooks, and Guardrails handle AI-specific risks, such as users trying to trick the “chef” into mistakes. Elastic scalability: Lambda clones itself as load grows, Auto Scaling adds or removes instances, and a load balancer shares the load. Figure 1. The title slide of Khang Duong’s talk, FCAJ member.
Figure 2. The agenda of From Prototype to Production by Khang Duong.
Figure 3. The restaurant story used throughout the talk.
Figure 4. AI as a feature inside an enterprise product.
Figure 5. The security pillar: KMS, IAM, and Guardrails.
Figure 6. The elastic scalability pillar: Lambda, Auto Scaling, and a load balancer.
2. AI in Enterprise and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore In the second part, Nguyen Lam Anh presented three challenges of bringing AI agents into an enterprise:
Security & Scalability: what can the agent touch, and how much load can it take? Integration & Context: can the agent work with real systems and keep context? Observability & Evaluation: do we know what the agent is doing, and is it right? The speaker then placed AgentCore in the overall picture: the model understands and responds, the agent application coordinates the model with tools (such as an order system), and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides managed capabilities for agents.
The most practical example for me was a hybrid design connected to Mobileye services: the ticket system runs on premises and cannot be reached from AWS. A local orchestrator pulls tickets and posts replies. The support agent runs on AgentCore Runtime, gets credentials from Secrets Manager so they are never exposed, and calls internal services through MCP for live status, logs, and errors. AgentCore Observability traces the full path from the request through the MCP tool calls to the reply. As a result, there is no inbound path into the on-premises network, yet the agent still has live data at inference time.
The part closed with the idea that agents do not throw errors like traditional software, so every run needs to be observed and graded. Each step (inputs, outputs, latency, tokens) is traced, and results are evaluated with code checks, LLM-as-a-judge, and red teaming.
Figure 7. Part 2 by Nguyen Lam Anh, AI Engineer at FCAJ.
Figure 8. Three challenges of bringing AI agents into an enterprise.
Figure 9. Where AgentCore sits relative to the model and the agent application.
Figure 10. A hybrid design that connects on-premises tickets to a cloud agent.
3. AgentCore components The third part went through each component in detail:
Identity: AgentCore separates inbound and outbound authentication, described as “two different doors, two different locks.” Inbound answers who the user is and whether they may call the agent; outbound answers whether the agent is who it claims to be and whether it may access a resource on behalf of the user. At run time, the agent holds a workload access token tied to both the agent and the user. Gateway: a shared connection point between many agents (customer support, shopping, pricing) and APIs, tools, and resources, with MCP support, tool creation and search, fine-grained access control, private connectivity, and tool filtering. The authorization flow starts with an inbound OAuth token (for example, authenticated through Amazon Cognito), after which the Gateway exchanges a workload access token for an outbound OAuth token to call the API. AgentCore Identity acts as the secure token vault. Memory: among the parts of the context window (system prompt, RAG documents, tools, instructions, message history), memory is often overlooked, yet without it agents miss learning and personalization. AgentCore Memory has short-term memory that stores raw interactions and long-term memory that stores extracted insights in a vector store. It is serverless, integrated with CloudWatch, lets short-term events expire after up to 365 days, supports namespaces, and encrypts data at rest and in transit. The agent writes messages and state to short-term memory synchronously, while an automatic extraction module runs asynchronously to move information into long-term memory using strategies such as semantic, user preferences, summarization, episodic, or a custom strategy. Observability: “you cannot fix what you cannot see.” Observability supports compliance, traceability, cost visibility, root-cause analysis in non-deterministic flows, latency tracking, and continuous evaluation. AgentCore collects OpenTelemetry data from the agent and from services such as Memory, Identity, and Gateway, then shows it on dashboards or sends it to third-party observability tools. Figure 11. AgentCore Identity separates inbound and outbound authentication.
Figure 12. AgentCore Gateway as a shared connection point between agents and tools.
Figure 13. The authorization flow in AgentCore Gateway.
Figure 14. Memory is often overlooked when building context for agents.
Figure 15. Short-term and long-term memory in AgentCore Memory.
Figure 16. How the agent writes to and retrieves from short-term and long-term memory.
Figure 17. Why AI agents need observability.
Figure 18. AgentCore Observability collects telemetry from the agent and AgentCore services.
4. Demo: from agent to deployment architecture The final part demonstrated a complete agent system. Strands Agents handled controlled orchestration: a request goes through FastAPI, a router sends it to the right agent (such as a Q&A agent, a ticket agent, or a research agent), and important actions pass an approval step before the result is returned. Langfuse was used to trace workflows and tool calls, investigate latency and failures, and observe model usage.
The deployment architecture on AWS included images stored in Amazon ECR, agents running on Amazon ECS with Fargate in private subnets across two Availability Zones, an Application Load Balancer for incoming requests, NAT gateways for outbound connections, Amazon Bedrock for models, Amazon DynamoDB for data, and Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring. Security relied on IAM and Secrets Manager, and cost optimization used Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets.
This architecture reuses many components I have practiced: a two-tier public/private VPC with a NAT gateway (Lab03), IAM and KMS (Module 05), DynamoDB (Lab60, Lab39), and AWS Budgets (Lab07). The difference is that everything is combined around a specific AI problem, with monitoring and cost control built into the design.
Figure 19. Controlled agent orchestration with Strands Agents.
Figure 20. Using Langfuse to observe the agent during the demo.
Figure 21. The deployment architecture of the agent system on AWS from the demo.
Key takeaways A working prototype is not a product yet: An enterprise AI system needs security, scalability, integration, and monitoring from the start, not as an afterthought. Security for AI goes beyond IAM: Besides encryption and permissions, AI-specific risks such as prompt injection must be considered, and the user’s permissions must be kept separate from the agent’s. Do not hide credentials in code: Use Secrets Manager or a token vault so the agent fetches credentials when needed. Agents need to be observed and graded: An agent can give a wrong answer without raising an error, so every step should be traced and results evaluated regularly. Memory is part of the design: Separate what needs to be remembered within a session from what must be kept long term, with retention periods and encryption. Applying to work For my personal workshop, I will use the four questions from this event to review my architecture: how the data is protected, how the system scales as load grows, how the components integrate, and how I know the system is working correctly. Secrets will be managed with Secrets Manager instead of being written in code or environment variables.
The testing and monitoring section of my workshop will go beyond CloudWatch logs and metrics and include test cases that check the output. If my workshop uses AI, I will record each processing step so that unexpected results can be traced.
Event experience The workshop covered a lot of content that was new to me, especially the AgentCore components. The restaurant story in the first part helped me follow fairly abstract concepts, and the demo showed how the services come together into an architecture that actually runs. Many of the talks were given by members of the FCAJ community, which gave me a clearer idea of what I can achieve after my internship.
